blocks.text: 如果科学家能在几分钟而非几个月内发现关于阿尔茨海默病和帕金森病的新线索，会怎样？OpenAI、PerturbAI⁠（在新窗口中打开）与Scripps Research⁠（在新窗口中打开）携手合作，利用由 GPT‑Rosalind 驱动的数千个 AI 智能体⁠（在新窗口中打开），在短短 32 分钟内分析并解读了来自数百万个小鼠脑细胞⁠（在新窗口中打开）的现有实验数据。这些智能体将基因干扰的影响与科学文献中的发现联系起来，揭示了意想不到的生物学关联，可帮助科学家理解疾病并确定新疗法的研究方向。这项工作表明，AI 可以帮助研究人员更充分地挖掘大型生物学实验所揭示的信息。

blocks.text: 现代实验产生的数据量远超科学家能够深入研究的范围。研究人员如今可以改变数千个基因，并在数百万个细胞中测量其影响。但要理解这些结果对人类疾病意味着什么，就需要将复杂的实验发现与数十年来零散的科学知识联系起来。这正是 AI 可以帮助科学家发现原本可能被遗漏的有前景线索的地方。

blocks.text: “我们构建细胞图谱，是为了让其他科学家能够做出我们尚未想象的发现。AI 可以帮助更多研究人员探索这些资源，并将意外的观察转化为有待检验的新问题。”
——Sarah Teichmann 博士，剑桥大学干细胞医学讲席教授、人类细胞图谱创始联合主席

inlines.text: ——Sarah Teichmann 博士，剑桥大学干细胞医学讲席教授、人类细胞图谱创始联合主席

blocks.text: 团队将分析任务分配给由 GPT‑Rosalind 驱动的数千个 AI 智能体，我们将这种方法称为分布式生物学推理。这些智能体检查了一个全脑 CRISPR 图谱⁠（在新窗口中打开），该数据集展示了基因干扰如何影响小鼠大脑中不同类型的细胞。每个智能体负责研究一个基因干扰，分析细胞反应，检索科学文献，并为结果提出解释。它们的报告被汇总成一个推理图谱，将基因、细胞效应、相关出版物和可能的生物学机制联系起来。

blocks.text: 研究团队估计，若由人类逐个干扰进行分析和文献综述，同等规模的工作将需要数月到一年时间。这些智能体复现了人类分析的发现，同时揭示了更多线索。它们对新颖性和科学价值的评估也与盲审人类专家的判断一致。这些发现有助于确定后续实验的优先级，以检验所提出的生物学机制。

blocks.text: 其中一些洞见为理解脑部疾病指明了新线索。这些智能体发现了两个与疾病相关的基因如何以不同方式影响脑细胞的意外差异，以及胆固醇调节与神经退行性变之间可能存在的关联。这些发现有助于科学家研究疾病如何发展，以及未来治疗可能在何处介入。

blocks.text: “有时线索已经存在，只是散落在不同领域——我们只是尚未将它们联系起来。神经元功能与胆固醇代谢之间可能存在的联系表明，一旦将这些片段汇集起来，就能为我们提供一种思考疾病生物学的新方式。”
——Tomasz Nowakowski，博士，加州大学旧金山分校神经外科副教授

inlines.text: ——Tomasz Nowakowski，博士，加州大学旧金山分校神经外科副教授

blocks.text: 研究人员现在就可以开始探索这些发现。推理图谱已开放获取⁠（在新窗口中打开），使科学家能够比较相关基因、研究意外反应，并找出值得追踪的有前景线索。当来自不同领域的研究人员汇聚各自的专业知识，并以意想不到的方式将熟悉的观点联系起来时，新发现往往就会涌现。AI 可以通过将新数据与散落在各学科的知识联系起来，大幅扩展这些连接。这一机遇不仅在于更快地分析数据。通过将 AI 与实验生物学、人类专业知识和科学文献相结合，我们可以帮助科学家将更多数据转化为可检验的想法。

blocks.text: 这些智能体发现了 Tsc1 与 Tsc2 之间的意外差异，这两个基因协同作用，共同调控 mTOR——细胞生长、代谢和衰老的主要调节因子。破坏其中任一基因，在若干组神经元中产生了相似的效果。但在协助协调运动的小脑中，破坏 Tsc2 改变了数十个参与神经元通讯的基因的活性，而破坏 Tsc1 则几乎没有产生变化。

inlines.text: 这些智能体发现了 Tsc1 与 Tsc2 之间的意外差异，这两个基因协同作用，共同调控 mTOR——细胞生长、代谢和衰老的主要调节因子。破坏其中任一基因，在若干组神经元中产生了相似的效果。但在协助协调运动的小脑中，破坏 Tsc2 改变了数十个参与神经元通讯的基因的活性，而破坏 Tsc1 则几乎没有产生变化。

blocks.text: 这一差异可能与人类疾病相关。在结节性硬化症患者中，小脑异常与 TSC2 突变密切相关。虽然降低 mTOR 活性的药物可以治疗某些脑肿瘤和癫痫发作，但与该疾病相关的学习和行为困难仍然难以应对。这些智能体 pinpoint 了一组值得研究的特定神经元和细胞变化：哪些变化可能被现有药物纠正，哪些可能指向新的治疗方法？这为研究人员提供了一组更具体的问题，可在实验室中检验。

inlines.text: 分工协作，深化推理

blocks.text: 一个获得完整数据集的单一智能体，能否与数千个并行工作的智能体表现一样好？我们在保持模型和资源不变的情况下对此进行了测试。随着工作量增加，单一智能体检索的文献更少，在最大工作量时仅引用了 11 篇参考文献，而分布式智能体引用了 700 多篇参考文献。人类专家也更倾向于分布式智能体给出的解读。

blocks.text: 科学家时间有限，往往只关注数据中最强的信号。分布式智能体有助于考察更广泛的响应，包括细微或意外的响应，并将它们与相关科学文献联系起来。并行运行这些智能体可以同时研究许多扰动。这有助于科学家探索实验中更多的内容，并识别出原本可能被遗漏的有希望的线索。

blocks.text: DCTN1参与神经元内部的货物运输。在全脑CRISPR图谱中，破坏Dctn1会增加参与胆固醇合成的基因的表达。智能体将这一观察与表明胆固醇运输问题可能导致细胞合成更多胆固醇的研究联系起来。这为后续实验提出了一个问题：DCTN1破坏是否会改变胆固醇在神经元内的分布，这些变化是否会导致神经退行性变？如果是这样，恢复正常的胆固醇分布是否有助于保护神经元？

blocks.text: What if scientists could uncover new clues about Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s in minutes instead of months? Working together, OpenAI, PerturbAI⁠(opens in a new window), and Scripps Research⁠(opens in a new window) used thousands of AI agents powered by GPT‑Rosalind⁠(opens in a new window) to analyze and interpret existing experimental data from millions of mouse brain cells⁠(opens in a new window) in just 32 minutes. The agents connected the effects of gene disruptions with findings from scientific literature, uncovering unexpected biological connections that can help scientists understand disease and identify research directions for new treatments. The work shows how AI can help researchers explore more of what large biological experiments reveal.

blocks.text: Modern experiments generate far more data than scientists can thoroughly investigate. Researchers can now alter thousands of genes and measure their effects across millions of cells. But understanding what these results mean for human disease requires connecting complex experimental findings with decades of scattered scientific knowledge. This is where AI can help scientists uncover promising leads that might otherwise be missed.

blocks.text: “We build cell atlases so that other scientists can make discoveries we haven’t imagined yet. AI could help more researchers explore these resources and turn unexpected observations into new questions to test.”
—Sarah Teichmann, Ph.D., Chair in Stem Cell Medicine at the University of Cambridge and founding co-chair of the Human Cell Atlas

inlines.text: —Sarah Teichmann, Ph.D., Chair in Stem Cell Medicine at the University of Cambridge and founding co-chair of the Human Cell Atlas

blocks.text: The team divided the analysis among thousands of AI agents powered by GPT‑Rosalind, an approach we call distributed biological reasoning. The agents examined a whole-brain CRISPR atlas⁠(opens in a new window), a dataset showing how gene disruptions affect different types of cells across the mouse brain. Each agent investigated a gene disruption, analyzed cellular responses, searched scientific literature, and proposed explanations for the results. Their reports were combined into a reasoning atlas linking genes, cellular effects, relevant publications, and possible biological mechanisms.

Each agent investigated a gene disruption, analyzed cellular responses, searched scientific literature, and proposed explanations for the results. Their reports were combined into a reasoning atlas linking genes, cellular effects, relevant publications, and possible biological mechanisms.

blocks.text: The research team estimated that comparable human analysis and literature review, conducted one perturbation at a time, would take months to a year. The agents reproduced findings from human analyses while uncovering additional leads. Their assessments of novelty and scientific value also aligned with judgments from blinded human experts. These findings help prioritize further experiments needed to test the proposed biological mechanisms.

blocks.text: Some of these insights point to new leads for understanding brain disease. The agents identified unexpected differences in how two disease-linked genes affect brain cells differently, as well as a potential connection between cholesterol regulation and neurodegeneration. These findings could help scientists investigate how disease develops and where future treatments might intervene.

blocks.text: Researchers can begin exploring these findings today. The reasoning atlas is available⁠(opens in a new window), allowing scientists to compare related genes, investigate unexpected responses, and identify promising leads to pursue. New discoveries often emerge when researchers from different fields bring their expertise together and connect familiar ideas in unexpected ways. AI can significantly scale these connections by linking new data with knowledge scattered across disciplines. The opportunity goes beyond analyzing data faster. By combining AI with experimental biology, human expertise, and scientific literature, we can help scientists turn more of their data into testable ideas.

blocks.text: Some of an experiment’s most interesting clues lie outside the story scientists set out to investigate. In a dataset spanning thousands of perturbations, those clues can be easy to miss.

blocks.text: The agents identified an unexpected difference between Tsc1 and Tsc2, two genes that work together to control mTOR, a major regulator of cell growth, metabolism, and aging. Disrupting either gene had similar effects in several groups of neurons. But in the cerebellum, which helps coordinate movement, Tsc2 disruption altered the activity of dozens of genes involved in neuronal communication, while Tsc1 disruption produced little change.

blocks.text: That difference may be relevant to human disease. In people with tuberous sclerosis, abnormalities in the cerebellum are strongly linked to TSC2 mutations. While medicines that reduce mTOR activity can treat certain brain tumors and seizures, learning and behavioral difficulties associated with the disease remain challenging to address. The agents pinpointed a specific group of neurons and cellular changes worth investigating: which changes might existing medicines correct, and which might point to new treatment approaches? This gives researchers a more specific set of questions to test in the lab.

blocks.text: Divide the work, deepen the reasoning

inlines.text: Divide the work, deepen the reasoning

blocks.text: Could a single agent given the entire dataset do just as well as thousands of agents working in parallel? We tested this while keeping the model and resources fixed. As the workload grew, the single agent searched less of the literature, citing only 11 references at the largest workload, while the distributed agents cited more than 700 references. Human experts also preferred the distributed-agent interpretations.

blocks.text: Scientists have limited time and often focus on the strongest signals in their data. Distributed agents can help examine a wider range of responses, including subtle or unexpected ones, and connect them with relevant scientific literature. Running the agents in parallel allows many perturbations to be investigated at once. This helps scientists explore more of what an experiment contains and identify promising leads that might otherwise be missed.

blocks.text: Finding the next experiment worth doing

inlines.text: Finding the next experiment worth doing

blocks.text: A finding becomes more valuable when it points to an experiment worth doing. The agents found one such lead in DCTN1, a gene whose mutations cause Perry syndrome, a neurodegenerative disease with Parkinson-like symptoms.

inlines.text: A finding becomes more valuable when it points to an experiment worth doing. The agents found one such lead in
DCTN1
, a gene whose mutations cause Perry syndrome, a neurodegenerative disease with Parkinson-like symptoms.

blocks.text: DCTN1 is involved in moving cargo inside neurons. In the whole-brain CRISPR atlas, disrupting Dctn1 increased the expression of genes involved in making cholesterol. The agents connected this observation with research suggesting that problems with cholesterol transport may cause cells to make more cholesterol. This raised a question for follow-up experiments: could DCTN1 disruption change how cholesterol is distributed within neurons, and could those changes contribute to neurodegeneration? If so, could restoring normal cholesterol distribution help protect neurons?

blocks.text: Scientists remain at the center of discovery. By uncovering more promising leads, AI can help researchers decide which ideas to pursue, design experiments, and interpret results. The goal is to turn more of the information in biological experiments into knowledge that, over time, can help guide the development of better medicines.
